title: Buying Property Safely: Documents, Ownership and Wills
summary: What to check before buying land or a house, and how ownership, inheritance and wills work.

body.text: Land and houses are the largest purchase most families make. A little checking before you pay saves years of dispute later.
Documents to check before you buy

items: Mother deed and the chain of title, showing how ownership passed over the years.
The latest encumbrance certificate (EC) from the sub-registrar, to see loans or claims on the property.
Patta / khata and property tax receipts in the seller's name.
Approved plan and layout approval, and whether the land is agricultural or residential.
Project approvals and RERA registration if you are buying from a builder.
Verify the seller's identity and that all legal heirs are on board.
Have a lawyer search the title for at least 30 years.
Sign a written agreement, pay through bank transfer, and keep receipts.
Register the sale deed at the sub-registrar's office and pay the stamp duty.
Update mutation and property tax records in your name.

body.text: Never pay a large advance on the strength of a photocopy or a power of attorney you have not verified. An unregistered agreement can leave you without an enforceable title.

items: If a person dies without a will (intestate), property passes to legal heirs under their personal law.
A will lets a person decide who gets what; it should be signed and witnessed.
A probate or succession certificate may be needed to transfer some assets.
A nomination in a bank account or insurance policy is not the same as inheritance.

body.text: Registration of a sale deed is compulsory for immovable property above the value set by law. An unregistered deed may not be accepted as proof of ownership.
Keep every original document in a safe place, and keep certified copies separately.

practicalSteps: Get an encumbrance certificate and a title search done before you pay.
Match the property description and measurements in the documents with the actual site.
Pay through banking channels and insist on written receipts.
Register the deed and collect the original document after registration.
exceptions: Buying agricultural land can carry state-specific restrictions on who may purchase it.
Inheritance rules differ by religion under the relevant personal law.

faqs.a: It is risky. Courts have held that a sale through an unregistered power of attorney may not transfer valid title. Insist on a registered deed.
It depends on the asset, the will and the state. For high-value or disputed estates, probate is often required.

sources.label: Transfer of Property Act, 1882 - India Code
RERA - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

misconceptions.myth: A notarised agreement is enough to own property.
misconceptions.fact: For immovable property, a registered sale deed is generally required; notarisation alone does not transfer ownership.
